title: Ego4D: Around the World in 3,000 Hours of Egocentric Video
tldr: 3,670 hours of unscripted first-person life from 931 wearers in 9 countries, with a benchmark suite split by tense: past, present, future.

problem.task: A benchmark suite over first-person video: episodic memory (past), hand-object and social interaction (present), forecasting (future).

inputs.name: egocentric video
inputs.chars: Unscripted daily life, minutes to hours, hundreds of scenarios.

inputs.name: side channels
inputs.chars: Present on subsets, not everywhere — a practical constraint people underestimate.

outputs.name: per-benchmark labels
outputs.chars: Query response windows, hand-object state changes, future actions.

training.note: Collection was designed around consent and de-identification, which is part of why it exists at this scale at all.

method.intuition: First-person video is a different distribution from web video — motion blur, out-of-frame hands, no editing — and the field could not study it without a corpus of this size.

metrics: per-track: recall, mAP, edit distance, success
experiments.headline: Baselines across five tracks, most of them far from usable, which is the point of releasing it.

why: The dataset that made the human-embodiment branch of physical AI a field rather than a handful of lab captures.

title: Ego-Exo4D: Understanding Skilled Human Activity from First- and Third-Person Perspectives
tldr: 1,286 hours of skilled activity filmed from the doer's eyes and from the outside at the same time, with coaches narrating what the performer is doing wrong.

problem.task: Fine-grained activity understanding, proficiency estimation, ego-exo cross-view translation, and 3D hand/body pose over skilled activity.

inputs.name: paired ego + exo video
inputs.chars: Simultaneous capture, 1–42 minute takes, 123 natural scenes.

inputs.name: language
inputs.chars: Coaches and teachers commenting on execution quality — the rare part.

training.supervision: Multiple paired language descriptions plus dense benchmark annotations.
training.note: Expert commentary is what makes proficiency and feedback tasks possible. Almost no other corpus has it.

method.intuition: Guidance systems have to see what the performer sees and judge it the way an outside expert would, so the two views must be captured together.
components: multichannel audio, gaze, IMU, point clouds, camera poses

experiments.headline: Baselines across four benchmark families, with cross-view tasks the least solved.

why: The bridge dataset between watching a person and coaching one, and the source of most skill-feedback work on this list.

title: Rescaling Egocentric Vision: Collection, Pipeline and Challenges for EPIC-KITCHENS-100
tldr: 100 hours of unscripted kitchen activity with 90K action segments, and a test-of-time split that asks whether a 2018 model still works on 2020 footage.

problem.task: Action recognition, detection, anticipation, cross-modal retrieval, and unsupervised domain adaptation across a two-year gap.

outputs.name: verb + noun
outputs.chars: Compositional action labels; the long tail is the difficulty.

training.supervision: Narration-driven annotation pipeline giving 54% denser actions per minute than the previous version.
training.note: The re-annotation pipeline itself is the methodological contribution — dense fine-grained labels from speech.

method.intuition: Egocentric action is compositional and long-tailed, and only unscripted collection at scale exposes that.

experiments.headline: Six tracks with defined baselines. Anticipation and domain adaptation remain the hard ones.

why: The long-running benchmark that most egocentric numbers on this list are reported against.

title: HD-EPIC: A Highly-Detailed Egocentric Video Dataset
tldr: 263 annotations per minute of unscripted kitchen video, all grounded in a digital twin of the room. Gemini Pro scores 38.5% on the resulting VQA.

problem.task: VQA over recipes, ingredients, nutrition, fine-grained actions, 3D perception, object motion and gaze; plus action, sound and long-term VOS.

inputs.name: egocentric video
inputs.chars: 41 h across 9 real home kitchens, unscripted.

training.supervision: Manual annotation grounded in 3D via digital twinning of fixtures and object locations, primed with gaze.
training.note: In-the-wild collection with lab-grade label density — the combination is what is new.

method.intuition: Annotation density and 3D grounding, not more hours, are what expose how little current models track about a scene.

baselines: Gemini Pro and other long-context VLMs
experiments.headline: Gemini Pro reaches only 38.5% on the VQA benchmark.

why: Sets the bar for what "grounded in the physical world" means for an annotation, and shows current VLMs are nowhere near it.

title: Assembly101: A Large-Scale Multi-View Video Dataset for Understanding Procedural Activities
tldr: People assembling and disassembling toy vehicles with no instructions, so the mistakes and corrections are real. It is the first dataset that proposed detecting them.

problem.task: Action recognition, anticipation, temporal segmentation, and the newly proposed mistake detection.

inputs.name: multi-view video
inputs.chars: 8 static plus 4 egocentric cameras, simultaneous — the first dataset with both.

outputs.name: mistake flag
outputs.chars: Ordering errors and corrections, occurring naturally because participants had no script.

training.supervision: Manual action segments plus 18M 3D hand poses.
training.note: Generalization to unseen toys is an explicit split, which is rarer than it should be.

method.intuition: If you hand people instructions you get clean data and no errors. Taking the instructions away is what produces a mistake dataset.

baselines: temporal segmentation and recognition models, pose vs. appearance
experiments.headline: Benchmarks across three tasks plus mistake detection, with cross-view and unseen-toy generalization studies.

why: The origin point for procedural mistake detection, and still the most-used evaluation for it.

title: HoloAssist: an Egocentric Human Interaction Dataset for Interactive AI Assistants in the Real World
tldr: Records what a human assistant actually does — 350 instructor-performer pairs, one wearing the headset, the other watching the feed and talking them through it.

problem.task: Mistake detection, intervention type prediction, and hand forecasting — framed around what a human instructor does.

inputs.name: seven synchronized streams
inputs.tensor: RGB, depth, head/hand/eye tracking, IMU, audio
inputs.chars: From a mixed-reality headset worn by the performer.

inputs.name: instructor speech
inputs.chars: Live verbal guidance, transcribed and typed by intervention category.

outputs.name: mistake / intervention
outputs.chars: Whether to intervene and how — correction, confirmation, warning.

training.supervision: Action and conversational annotations over 166 hours.
training.note: The instructor is a person, so intervention timing and phrasing are observed rather than designed.

method.intuition: Before building an assistant, record what human assistants do — when they interrupt, how they ground an instruction in the scene, how they recover a mistake.

experiments.headline: Baselines on all three tasks plus an analysis of how human assistants correct, intervene and ground instructions.

why: The reference recording of the interaction this whole branch is trying to automate.

title: CaptainCook4D: A Dataset for Understanding Errors in Procedural Activities
tldr: 94.5 hours of real cooking where half the recordings deliberately induce errors, so a mistake detector has positive examples that were not staged after the fact.

problem.task: Supervised error recognition, multi-step localization, and procedure learning.

inputs.name: egocentric 4D recording
inputs.chars: 384 recordings in real kitchens; two conditions — following the recipe, and deviating from it.

inputs.name: recipe
inputs.chars: The reference procedure the execution is scored against.

training.note: Errors are induced by instruction rather than waited for, which trades ecological validity for label balance.

method.intuition: Errors are rare in natural recordings, so a usable error dataset has to be designed to contain them.

experiments.headline: Benchmarks for supervised error recognition, multi-step localization and procedure learning.

why: The standard evaluation for procedural error work, and the dataset most task-graph papers report on.

title: IndustReal: A Dataset for Procedure Step Recognition Handling Execution Errors in Egocentric Videos in an Industrial-Like Setting
tldr: Recognizing that an action happened is not the same as recognizing it worked. Procedure step recognition scores completion and order, and the test set holds out unseen mistakes.

problem.task: Procedure step recognition: did the step complete correctly, and in the right order?

inputs.name: egocentric video
inputs.chars: Industrial-like assembly of a physical kit; 3D models of all parts released.

outputs.name: assembly state
outputs.chars: Which parts are in place — the state, not the action.

outputs.name: step completion
outputs.chars: Includes procedural omissions and execution errors.

training.supervision: Annotated action, assembly state, and PSR labels.
training.note: A significant part of the errors appears only in validation and test, so robustness to unseen mistakes is measured rather than assumed.

method.intuition: Industrial value lies in the outcome, not the gesture, so the task should score completion instead of action identity.
components: public 3D part models for synthetic training

baselines: action recognition and state detection models
experiments.headline: Benchmark performance for action recognition, assembly state detection and the new PSR task, with released code and weights.

why: Reframes the human-verify problem from "what did they do" to "did the world reach the intended state".
